item.title: Efforts to preserve, promote iTaukei language

item.content:encoded:
For generations, knowledge has been passed down through talanoa, songs, and legends and now the iTaukei Trust Fund Board (TTFB) is turning that oral tradition into books for children.

The board opened its inaugural Talanoa BookLab yesterday at the Centre for Appropriate Technology and Development in Nadave, where 12 to 15 authors will work with Ministry of Education’s curriculum advisers and illustrators from August 31 to September 2.

The curriculum is aimed at students of Years 7 and 8.

The board’s senior program specialist, Unaisi Manulevu, said the project was about more than literacy.

“We are not only trying to preserve the language. We want the stories our children read to be culturally rooted and grounded and to help them understand who they are,” she said.

“We must go back to teaching our children not only to speak vosa vakaviti, but also to read it, write it and understand it.”

The initiative forms part of the board’s ongoing work to preserve and promote the iTaukei language and culture, and to ensure vosa vakaviti continues to be spoken, read, written and understood by future generations.

The stories will focus on themes such as climate change, nature, bula vaka vanua and vai tovo vaka vanua, helping young readers connect with their culture and environment.

Among those involved is illustrator Anare Somumu, who will guide the visual development of the stories on the final day.

After the workshop, the stories will go through the board’s publishing process before being printed as supplementary reading material.

item.title: Woman fined $200
item.description: A LABASA businesswoman has been fined $200 for dumping commercial waste into a public rubbish bin. Sky Tech Investment owner Shahimma Bi Khan pleaded guilty to one count of depositing commercial waste into a receptacle provided for public use, under the Litter Act 2008, when she appeared in the Labasa Magistrate’s Court.
item.content:encoded:
A LABASA businesswoman has been fined $200 for dumping commercial waste into a public rubbish bin.

Sky Tech Investment owner Shahimma Bi Khan pleaded guilty to one count of depositing commercial waste into a receptacle provided for public use, under the Litter Act 2008, when she appeared in the Labasa Magistrate’s Court.

The court heard that Ms Khan was seen at Nasekula, Labasa, on December 11, 2025, putting cartons and other rubbish from her business into a bin meant for public use.

Resident Magistrate Amelia Korodau said the rubbish came from Ms Khan’s business, and she was responsible for making sure her commercial waste was properly disposed of.

The court heard that Ms Khan, 34, is a sole trader and, therefore, responsible for providing the required facilities to manage waste from her business.

She was ordered to pay a $200 fine within 14 days, but would be jailed for 20 days if she failed to pay up.

The court noted that Ms Khan had no previous convictions, pleaded guilty at an early stage and was remorseful for the offence.

The maximum fine for an individual under the Act is $200, while a company can be fined up to $1000.

The court also warned Ms Khan that any further offence could result in a much higher fine.

item.title: Jail sentence for assaulting wife
item.description: A man was sentenced to seven months imprisonment for violently assaulting his wife after demanding money, meant for their sick baby’s hospital visit, to buy alcohol. The 34-year-old was convicted of assault after pleading guilty before Magistrate Samanunu Vaniqi.
item.content:encoded:
A man was sentenced to seven months imprisonment for violently assaulting his wife after demanding money, meant for their sick baby’s hospital visit, to buy alcohol.

The 34-year-old was convicted of assault after pleading guilty before Magistrate Samanunu Vaniqi.

The court heard that on June 11 this year, the man was drinking alcohol at home with friends when his wife informed him that their youngest child was sick. But the man, who was intoxicated at that time, demanded money to buy more alcohol.

After an argument ensued over prioritising alcohol over their sick child, his wife handed him $100 intended for taking their son to the hospital. He instead entered a vehicle with another individual.

When questioned by his wife, the man pushed her aside and repeatedly punched her. Upon returning home, he continued the assault by punching her, throwing her against a wall, choking her, and directing vulgar language at her.

The man was ordered to serve three months in jail, with the remaining four months suspended for three years.

The court also issued a final Domestic Violence Restraining Order (DVRO) to protect the complainant.

item.title: Values through books | Calls for early action on social ills
item.description: VERNACULAR storybooks that teach children traditional values and morals could become an early tool to tackle crime, drug use and other social problems in iTaukei communities, says illustrator Anare Somumu. He made the comments at the iTaukei Language Literacy Through Short Story BookLab Talanoa, where authors, curriculum advisers and illustrators are developing stories aimed at primary school chil
item.content:encoded:
VERNACULAR storybooks that teach children traditional values and morals could become an early tool to tackle crime, drug use and other social problems in iTaukei communities, says illustrator Anare Somumu.

He made the comments at the iTaukei Language Literacy Through Short Story BookLab Talanoa, where authors, curriculum advisers and illustrators are developing stories aimed at primary school children.

Mr Somumu said the country’s social problems highlighted the need to start addressing these issues while children were still young.

“If you look at society, most of the woes point a finger at the iTaukei community,” he said.

“If you see crime, the majority is committed by iTaukei. If you go to the prisons, the majority are iTaukei. If you see drugs, you’ll see that iTaukei are involved.”

Mr Somumu said while changing adults could be difficult, literature could help shape the values and behaviour of the next generation.

“I believe writing books or producing books could be a way for us writers and illustrators contribute towards these issues from a very early age.

“It’s a bit hard to change those who are now adults, but for the next generations, we need to do this more.”

He said the books should not be limited to teaching children to read and write in vosa vakaviti, but should also instil values and morals.

“Not only write books for them to learn vernacular reading but also instil values and morals in the stories so that it also helps build our children.”

Mr Somumu, one of the illustrators selected for the project, will develop illustration briefs for the stories on the final day of the BookLab.

He said the books could also strengthen iTaukei identity by reconnecting children with traditional stories, legends and cultural knowledge.

item.title: Fertility rate falls
item.description: FIJI’S fertility rate has fallen to 2.27 children per woman, highlighting a major shift towards smaller families and slower population growth. University of the South Pacific lecturer in Population and Demography Dr Sumeet Lal said Fiji had experienced a sustained decline in fertility over several decades.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI’S fertility rate has fallen to 2.27 children per woman, highlighting a major shift towards smaller families and slower population growth.

University of the South Pacific lecturer in Population and Demography Dr Sumeet Lal said Fiji had experienced a sustained decline in fertility over several decades.

“In the late 20th century, women in Fiji had an average of approximately 4 children,” Dr Lal said.

“By the early 2000s, fertility had fallen to around three children per woman, and by 2024 it had declined further to 2.27 children per woman, only slightly above replacement level.”

The decline has been accompanied by a sharp fall in the country’s birth rate.

Dr Lal said the crude birth rate had fallen from approximately 34 births per 1000 population in the late 20th century to about 24 per 1000 in the early 2000s and 18 per 1000 in 2024.

“As fewer children are born each year, the share of young people within the population naturally tends to decline.”

The impact is already visible in Fiji’s age structure.

About 47 per cent of the population was under 18 in 1980, compared with 32.7 per cent in 2023.

He said Fiji’s median age had also increased from 18.3 years in 1980 to 27.7 years in 2023.

“Today, Fiji continues to grow, but rather at a much more modest pace, with a population structure characterised by smaller family sizes, a rising median age, and a lower proportion of children than in previous generations.”

According to Mr Lal, Fiji’s annual population growth rate, which exceeded two per cent in the late 20th century, declined to around one per cent in the early 2000s and approximately 0.52 per cent by 2023.

item.title: Vacant teaching posts to be filled
item.description: A TOTAL of 130 vacant teaching positions in the country’s 738 primary and 176 secondary schools will soon be filled. Fiji Teachers Union general secretary Muniappa Gounder said following a meeting with senior Ministry of Education officials last Thursday, union members were assured the ministry would begin their search to fill the vacant posts.
item.content:encoded:
A TOTAL of 130 vacant teaching positions in the country’s 738 primary and 176 secondary schools will soon be filled.

Fiji Teachers Union general secretary Muniappa Gounder said following a meeting with senior Ministry of Education officials last Thursday, union members were assured the ministry would begin their search to fill the vacant posts.

“The Fiji Teachers Union welcomes the outcome of its meeting with officials of the Ministry of Education held on Thursday, 27 August 2026, where it was agreed that all substantively vacant teaching positions in both primary and secondary schools will be advertised on Saturday, 29 August 2026,” said Mr Gounder.

“The positions to be advertised comprise 37 secondary school positions, including five large, four medium and 28 small school positions, and 93 primary school positions, comprising six large, 21 medium and 66 small school positions.”

He said the union considered this a welcome and long overdue development.

“Particularly in addressing the ongoing need to fill substantively vacant positions and strengthen staffing in schools across the country.

“Timely filling of these positions is important to ensure stability in schools and provide teachers with appropriate opportunities for career progression and professional advancement.

“The union, therefore, strongly encourages all eligible and suitably qualified teachers to take advantage of this opportunity and submit their applications for the advertised positions.

“The FTU remains committed to working constructively with the Ministry of Education to address teacher-related issues and ensure that our schools are adequately staffed for the benefit of teachers and, most importantly, the children we serve.”

item.title: Racagi case back with ODPP
item.description: The investigation into the death of police constable Peni Racagi has taken a new turn, with forensic results from New Zealand now back in Fiji and the case file returned to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP). The Fiji Police Force confirmed the investigation file had been forwarded to the ODPP following receipt of the overseas forensic findings.
item.content:encoded:
The investigation into the death of police constable Peni Racagi has taken a new turn, with forensic results from New Zealand now back in Fiji and the case file returned to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP).

The Fiji Police Force confirmed the investigation file had been forwarded to the ODPP following receipt of the overseas forensic findings.

“The file is with ODPP, with the results that came from New Zealand,” police said.

Constable Racagi was found dead in Lami waters on February 22 this year after reportedly being on duty the night before.

Two men, aged 42 and 20, were charged with murder in March and appeared in court in connection with the death of the young officer.

However, the prosecution did not proceed after the ODPP determined there was insufficient evidence at the time to continue with the case.

Samples and specimens linked to the investigation were subsequently sent to New Zealand for specialised forensic examination, as the equipment required for the testing was not available in Fiji.

The return of those results has now allowed police to complete the investigation file and submit it back to prosecutors.

The ODPP will assess the new forensic findings together with the other evidence gathered during the investigation before deciding whether further action should be taken.

At this stage, no new charge has been announced.

The latest development would determine the next course of action in the investigation into the death of Constable Racagi.

item.title: BACK IN HISTORY | RB opens new shop
item.description: R B Patel opened its vast new Centerpoint Supermarket at Laucala Beach Estate, described as second to none in Fiji, with space for 140 cars and 10 shops. The Fiji Times reported on Sunday, May 11, 1986, that it was as if a city had moved out to the suburbs.
item.content:encoded:
R B Patel opened its vast new Centerpoint Supermarket at Laucala Beach Estate, described as second to none in Fiji, with space for 140 cars and 10 shops.

The Fiji Times reported on Sunday, May 11, 1986, that it was as if a city had moved out to the suburbs.

The new complex included a 30,000sq foot supermarket, the largest in Fiji at the time, a 35,000sq foot bulk warehouse, 10 specialty shops, a children’s playground and parking for 140 cars.

Ambu Patel, the manager of Centerpoint at that time, said he had studied overseas designs to plan the store.

“I spent many hours overseas researching the best points of supermarkets and hypermarkets available and used that information to design the new supermarket,” he said

He said the wide aisles were designed to avoid crowding.

“The aisles were wide enough to accommodate three trolleys abreast without causing the traffic jams common in most other supermarkets.”

He said more services were planned for the complex.

“We were also going to have a hairdresser, a pharmacist, a doctor, a butcher and a greengrocer.”

He said the store would also compete on price.

“RB’s promised to undercut any competitor’s advertised price to remain the cheapest around.”

Centerpoint marked a new era of suburban shopping in Fiji in the 1980s, and offered size, variety, and modern facilities to make retail more convenient for Lautoka families.
